claimants.description: Morocco claims Western Sahara as part of its territory.
The Polisario Front seeks an independent Sahrawi state and proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.

administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Morocco administers most of the territory west of the berm.
The Polisario Front controls territory east of the berm; the authority does not encode that control line.

internationalStatus.summary: The territory remains on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories and its final status is unresolved.

perspectives.statement: The United Nations lists Western Sahara as a Non-Self-Governing Territory and maintains a settlement mission.

explanation.summary: Morocco administers most of Western Sahara and claims it as Moroccan. The Polisario Front seeks an independent Sahrawi state. The territory’s final status remains unresolved.
explanation.claims: Morocco claims Western Sahara as part of its territory. The Polisario Front, which proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, seeks independence for it.
explanation.administration: Morocco administers most of the territory, west of the fortified sand wall known as the berm. The Polisario Front controls territory to its east. This is a broad description, not a map of today’s military positions.
explanation.disputeReason: Spain’s withdrawal did not settle the territory’s future. Western Sahara remains on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories, and the UN political process has not produced an agreed final settlement.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas keeps Western Sahara as one separately selectable territory. Its outline shows that territory—not the berm, either side’s control, or a decision on sovereignty.

citations.supports: UN classification as a Non-Self-Governing Territory since 1963.
UN settlement proposals and ceasefire process involving Morocco and Frente POLISARIO.
Morocco’s administration of most of the territory and the unresolved UN-mediated dispute.
Distinguishes Moroccan-controlled territory from Polisario-controlled territory east of the berm; page checked 5 September 2026.
Spanish withdrawal, competing territorial claims and the Sahrawi independence movement.
The Polisario Front’s proclamation of the SADR. The AU is an organization that recognizes the SADR, not a neutral recognition registry.

claimants.description: Kosovo’s authorities claim an independent state following the 2008 declaration.
Serbia rejects Kosovo’s independence and maintains a territorial claim.

administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Kosovo’s institutions operate the government; this record does not infer a fine-grained control map.
Serbia-supported health and education services exist particularly for the Serb community.

internationalStatus.summary: Many states recognize Kosovo, but recognition is not universal and UNMIK continues on a status-neutral basis.

perspectives.statement: UNMIK continues under Security Council resolution 1244 on a status-neutral basis.

explanation.summary: Kosovo has its own government and declared independence in 2008. Serbia considers it part of Serbia. Many states recognize Kosovo, but international recognition is not universal.
explanation.claims: Kosovo’s authorities claim an independent state. Serbia rejects that independence and maintains its territorial claim.
explanation.administration: Kosovo’s institutions run its government. Serbia-supported services also exist, particularly for the Serb community; their relationship to Kosovo’s institutions is part of the EU-facilitated dialogue.
explanation.disputeReason: The 2008 independence declaration did not produce an agreed settlement with Serbia. UNMIK continues under Security Council resolution 1244 on a status-neutral basis.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas makes Kosovo separately selectable, following Natural Earth. That practical choice does not settle recognition or imply a division of control inside its boundary.

citations.supports: Resolution 1244 mandate and Kosovo’s post-2008 status context.
The independence declaration, Kosovo’s institutions and the changed role of UNMIK.
Kosovo institutions and Serbia-supported health and education services addressed by the dialogue.

claimants.description: Turkish Cypriot authorities claim a separate state in the north.
The Republic of Cyprus claims sovereignty over the island apart from the British sovereign base areas.

administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Turkish Cypriot authorities administer the north.
The Republic of Cyprus administers the south; a UN-patrolled buffer zone separates the two sides.

internationalStatus.summary: The self-declared state is recognized by Türkiye; Security Council resolution 541 called for non-recognition by other states.

perspectives.statement: Resolution 541 rejected the 1983 declaration and called for non-recognition.
Türkiye recognizes the self-declared state in the north.

explanation.summary: Northern Cyprus is run by Turkish Cypriot authorities, outside the Republic of Cyprus’s effective control. The self-declared state is recognized by Türkiye, but not by the UN as a separate Cypriot state.
explanation.claims: The Turkish Cypriot authorities claim a separate state. The Republic of Cyprus claims sovereignty over the island, apart from the British sovereign base areas.
explanation.administration: Turkish Cypriot authorities administer the north; the Republic of Cyprus administers the south. A UN-patrolled buffer zone separates the two sides.
explanation.disputeReason: Cyprus has been divided since the 1974 conflict. The north declared independence in 1983; UN Security Council resolution 541 rejected that declaration and called for non-recognition.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas draws the north separately so the island’s practical division is visible. It does not treat separate coloring as international recognition or show a detailed buffer-zone boundary.

citations.supports: The Security Council’s position on the 1983 declaration; this is distinct from the source’s cartographic ‘Sovereign country’ label.
The division, effective administration, buffer zone and Türkiye’s recognition.
Confirms that the north is outside the Republic of Cyprus’s control; checked 5 September 2026.

claimants.description: Somaliland’s authorities claim independence following the 1991 declaration.
Somalia considers Somaliland part of Somalia.

administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Somaliland’s authorities operate separately from Somalia’s federal government, but the claimed eastern boundary and actual control are not identical.

internationalStatus.summary: Recognition is not uniform; Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025 while Somalia and the Security Council maintained a territorial-integrity position.

perspectives.statement: The Security Council position cited in the briefing affirms Somalia’s territorial integrity.

explanation.summary: Somaliland has separate governing institutions and claims independence from Somalia. Somalia rejects that claim. Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025; recognition is not uniform.
explanation.claims: Somaliland’s authorities claim independence. Somalia considers the territory part of Somalia; the Security Council has repeatedly affirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity.
explanation.administration: Somaliland’s authorities operate separately from Somalia’s federal government. Its claimed eastern boundary and actual control are not identical; this map is not a current territorial-control survey.
explanation.disputeReason: Somaliland declared independence in 1991, but that did not lead to an agreed separation from Somalia. Israel’s December 2025 recognition changed one diplomatic relationship, not everyone’s position.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas retains the separate Natural Earth unit. Do not read its full outline as the present reach of Somaliland’s government, or its color as universal recognition.

citations.supports: Israel’s recognition, Somalia’s rejection and the Security Council position as reported on 29 December 2025.
Continuing conflict in the eastern regions; checked 5 September 2026.
The 1991 independence declaration and development of separate institutions. Its old recognition description is superseded by the 2025 evidence above.
The July 2025 country note distinguishes Somaliland administration from SSC-Khatumo control and other areas; Atlas does not reproduce these as current borders.

claimants.description: The statehood claim concerns the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza.
Israel claims East Jerusalem as part of its capital; the UN framework cited here does not recognize that annexation.

administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: The Palestinian Authority exercises limited administration in parts of the West Bank under Israeli occupation.

administratorsOrControllers.actorName: Authorities and military forces in Gaza
administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Administration and military control in Gaza are changing and fragmented; this authority stores prose, not a control-line geometry.

internationalStatus.summary: Palestine has UN non-Member Observer State status; recognition, borders, administration, occupation, and effective control remain distinct questions.

perspectives.statement: The UN lists Palestine as a non-Member Observer State and treats the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza as occupied Palestinian territory in the cited framework.

explanation.summary: Palestine comprises the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza in the UN’s territorial framework. It has UN observer-State status, but those territories do not function as one area under a single government’s control.
explanation.claims: Palestinian statehood claims concern the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza. Israel claims East Jerusalem as part of its capital; the UN does not recognize that annexation.
explanation.administration: The Palestinian Authority exercises limited administration in parts of the West Bank under Israeli occupation. Gaza’s administration and military control have been profoundly disrupted by war; the cited June 2026 UN report describes de facto authorities and Israeli military positions, not a single settled administration.
explanation.disputeReason: The UN treats the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza as occupied Palestinian territory. Observer-State status, recognition, borders and effective control are different questions; this map cannot answer them with one sovereign-name label.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas selects the West Bank and Gaza together as Palestine. It does not draw Areas A/B/C, settlements, the separation barrier or current Gaza control lines. The source’s ‘Israel’ sovereign-name field is not used as Atlas’s sovereignty judgment.

citations.supports: Palestine’s non-Member Observer State status under General Assembly resolution 67/19.
The 29 November 2012 observer-State decision and its territorial context.
Dated evidence of fragmented administration, de facto authorities and changing military control in Gaza.
Occupied-territory framework, East Jerusalem and Israeli settlement activity.
The occupied-territory framework and the legal distinction between administration, annexation and sovereignty in East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

claimants.description: The People’s Republic of China claims Taiwan as part of China but does not administer it.

administratorsOrControllers.actorName: Republic of China institutions in Taiwan
administratorsOrControllers.extentDescription: Taiwan elects its own president and legislature and runs courts and public services separately from the People’s Republic of China.

internationalStatus.summary: Self-government, diplomatic recognition, and other states’ One China policies are distinct questions.

perspectives.statement: The EU states a One China policy while maintaining relations with Taiwan.

explanation.summary: Taiwan is self-governed by the Republic of China’s institutions. The People’s Republic of China claims Taiwan as its territory but does not administer it. International recognition differs from this practical separation.
explanation.claims: The People’s Republic of China claims Taiwan as part of China. Taiwan’s government operates as the Republic of China; political views within Taiwan differ over its long-term relationship with the mainland.
explanation.administration: Taiwan elects its own president and legislature and runs its own courts and public services. These are separate from the People’s Republic of China’s institutions.
explanation.disputeReason: The Republic of China and the People’s Republic of China emerged on opposing sides of China’s civil war. Their competing positions, and other states’ different diplomatic policies, make self-government and international recognition distinct questions.
explanation.mapChoice: Taiwan is a separate selectable unit in Atlas. This lets its geography and available data be explored without treating the map’s color or inclusion as a sovereignty ruling.

citations.supports: One explicitly stated diplomatic position: the EU’s One China policy alongside its relations with Taiwan.
Taiwan’s separate elected institutions, PRC claim, ROC identity and differing international recognition.

records.scopeCaveat: This record describes only Natural Earth’s separately drawn Siachen Glacier map unit. It is not a model of all Kashmir, its competing claims, administration, or lines of control.

claimants.description: Natural Earth’s source record lists an Indian claim for this map unit.
Natural Earth’s source record lists a Pakistani claim for this map unit.

internationalStatus.summary: This bounded record preserves the locked map source’s Indeterminate classification; it does not attempt an international-status account of the wider Kashmir dispute.

perspectives.statement: The locked source draws Siachen Glacier separately, classifies it as Indeterminate, and notes claims by India and Pakistan.

explanation.summary: Siachen Glacier is a separately drawn geographic unit in this source, not a sovereign country. Natural Earth labels it ‘Indeterminate’ and records claims by India and Pakistan. Its outline is not a live military-control line.
explanation.claims: Natural Earth records claims by India and Pakistan for this specific Siachen Glacier map unit. Atlas does not expand that source note into a claim model for all Kashmir.
explanation.administration: This bounded authority does not identify a current administrator or encode military positions. Absence here means Atlas has not authored that claim, not that no control relationship exists.
explanation.disputeReason: Siachen is represented separately by the current geographic source. This record deliberately does not attempt to explain or spatially model the wider Kashmir dispute.
explanation.mapChoice: Atlas retains Natural Earth’s separately selectable Siachen Glacier outline. The outline is not all Kashmir and is not a current line-of-control map.

citations.supports: The locked source maps Siachen Glacier separately, classifies it as Indeterminate, and stores the note ‘Claimed by Pakistan and India’.
Natural Earth’s de facto cartographic policy is not a legal sovereignty determination.

review.note: Scope was narrowed explicitly to the source map unit so Atlas cannot imply that Siachen stands for all Kashmir.
